tasks.task_description: (a) Develop model(s) to explore the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint and identify the bottlenecks.
tasks.task_analysis: The checkpoint is modeled as a multi-zone, multi-lane queueing network. A passenger's end-to-end journey is decomposed into stages: (Zone A) arrival and ID check, (Zone B) lane entry and bag staging onto the X-ray belt, (Zone C) body scan (millimeter-wave) running in parallel with belt dwell, and (Zone D) secondary/exception screening (pat-down, bag search) entered probabilistically. Two lane families exist in parallel: 4 regular lanes and 1 TSA Pre-Check lane, with 45% of arriving passengers enrolled in Pre-Check. The core structural tension is that 45% of traffic is concentrated on a single Pre-Check lane while the remaining 55% spreads over four regular lanes, making the Pre-Check lane the candidate bottleneck. To identify bottlenecks rigorously, I use a hybrid approach (per expert round 1): an Agent-Based Discrete-Event Simulation (ABDES) as the primary lens, because only an agent-based model captures the parallel-lane interior, bag/body parallelism, exception rework, and pre-check/regular interaction that generate the congestion; and an M/G/c analytic layer as a supporting cross-check, reporting per-stage offered load, server count, utilization rho, and closed-form mean/variance of wait. Variance is defined throughout as the variance of end-to-end queueing delay (time waiting), not total process time, which is reported separately as a secondary metric (expert round 1).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Service-time distributions are fitted to the provided dataset (2017_ICM_Problem_D_Data.csv) and anchored to TSA service standards. ID check: lognormal(mu=2.3668, sigma=0.3282), mean 11.2 s, from both ID-check officer streams. Belt-to-belt dwell: lognormal(mu=3.2129, sigma=0.5799), mean 28.6 s, p90 48 s. Body scan: lognormal mean 45 s. Pat-down (Zone D): lognormal mean 90 s; bag search: lognormal mean 60 s. Arrivals are inhomogeneous Poisson over a 6-hour horizon with a Gaussian peak (center 110 min, sigma 70 min, base rate 0.25, peak 2.4 pax/min), implemented by thinning so the peak-window density is ~2.4-2.75 pax/min over 80-120 min. Lane service time for a passenger is belt_dwell + max(0, body_scan - belt_dwell) (body scan overlaps belt dwell); Pre-Check passengers get faster belt (x0.7) and body scan (x0.9). Light-load Pre-Check passengers (self-selected, fraction light_frac) get belt x0.5. The ABDES is an event-driven simulation: each passenger draws arrival time, lane type (Pre-Check with prob 0.45), exception probabilities (pat-down base 0.05, bag-flag base 0.03, both elevated for regular lanes), and per-stage service times; passengers queue at the ID-check stations (2 servers) and then at lane servers. Each replication uses n_arrivals=500; 5 seeds {3,7,11,13,17} are run and the per-replication passenger-level statistics are averaged across seeds. The M/G/c analytic layer computes, per stage, offered load A = lambda_stage * E[service] at the peak window, servers c, rho = A/c, and Erlang-C mean and variance of wait. The headline output is the within-replication passenger-level variance of end-to-end queueing delay (queue_wait_var), plus p50/p90/p99, the fraction within 10 min (Pre-Check TSA target) and 30 min (regular TSA target), and throughput per hour, each for the overall population and for the Pre-Check and regular sub-populations.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (no modifications): overall queueing-delay mean 7.91 min, variance 55.19 min^2, p50 ~2.5 min, p90 ~13 min, p99 23.58 min; 84% of all passengers wait <=10 min and 98% <=30 min. The analytic M/G/c layer identifies the bottleneck precisely: the Pre-Check stage has offered load A=0.72 with 1 server, rho=0.72, mean wait ~8 min and wait variance ~80 min^2; the regular stage has A=1.01 over 4 servers, rho=0.25, mean wait ~0.5 min; the ID-check stage has A=0.40 over 2 servers, rho=0.20. Thus the single Pre-Check lane is the clear bottleneck (rho 0.72 vs 0.25/0.20 elsewhere), even though it serves only 45% of traffic. The simulation confirms this: the Pre-Check sub-population has mean queueing delay 7.91 min, variance 80.13 min^2, p99 24.51 min, and only 66% within the 10-min Pre-Check TSA target — well below the 99% TSA standard — while the regular sub-population is healthy (p99 1.13 min, 100% within 30 min). The system meets the overall 30-min standard (98%) but fails the Pre-Check 10-min standard (66% vs 99%), and the Pre-Check lane is the source of both the variance and the standard violation. Bottleneck: the single Pre-Check lane (utilization ~0.72, high wait variance, standard miss). Secondary, non-binding: the ID-check stations (rho 0.20) and the regular lanes (rho 0.25) have headroom.

tasks.task_description: (b) Develop at least two modifications that improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them to demonstrate their impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Per expert round 2, I model two complementary, low-cost headline modifications: M1 (demand-side variance reduction) and M3 (supply-side variance reduction), plus a combined scenario. M1 targets the Pre-Check bottleneck directly: it adds a second Pre-Check lane (correcting the known 1:3 Pre-Check-to-regular lane ratio) and lets light-load Pre-Check passengers self-select into a faster belt-dwell sub-lane (belt x0.5), truncating the service-time upper tail. M3 is a policy change, not added labor: a dynamic lane-opening trigger opens a reserve regular lane when total queue length reaches a threshold and closes it when the queue drops to half the threshold, absorbing arrival surges. Both hold staffing fixed except where a modification explicitly changes lane configuration (M1 adds one Pre-Check lane; M3 opens/closes an otherwise-idle lane), so the gains are attributable to the modification. Per the expert, M1 is swept over the light-load self-selection fraction (not a single point) and M3 over the trigger threshold (rule fixed). Automated bag check is documented as future work because the belt-to-belt variance could not be cleanly attributed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1 is parameterized by light_frac in {0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50} with precheck_lanes=2: a fraction light_frac of Pre-Check passengers are flagged light-load and receive belt dwell scaled by 0.5; the remaining Pre-Check passengers keep belt x0.7. The second Pre-Check lane doubles Pre-Check server capacity, cutting Pre-Check offered load from A=0.72 (1 server) to ~0.36 (2 servers). M3 is parameterized by trigger_threshold in {3, 5, 8, 12}: a reserve regular lane is opened when the total waiting queue >= threshold and closed when <= threshold/2 (hysteresis to avoid flapping). M1+M3 combined uses light_frac=0.30, 2 Pre-Check lanes, and threshold=5. All scenarios run the same 5-seed ABDES protocol as the baseline; the reported metric is the cross-seed mean of per-replication passenger-level queueing-delay variance, with p99 and the 10/30-min compliance fractions.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: M1 is the dominant fix. Across the light-load fraction sweep, overall queueing-delay variance falls from the baseline 55.19 to 0.12-0.51 min^2 (a ~99% reduction), p99 falls from 23.58 to 1.25-4.70 min, and 100% of passengers are within 10 min. The Pre-Check sub-population is transformed: variance 80.13 -> ~0.3 min^2, p99 24.51 -> ~3 min, and 100% within the 10-min Pre-Check TSA target (up from 66%). The effect is large even at the smallest light-load fraction (0.10), because the second Pre-Check lane — not the express sub-lane — is what removes the bottleneck; the light-load express lane adds a further tail-truncation on top. M3 (dynamic trigger) helps more modestly and is threshold-sensitive: overall variance is 41.86 (th=3), 85.76 (th=5), 36.48 (th=8, best), and 55.33 (th=12) versus baseline 55.19. The non-monotonic response reflects the hysteresis: a low threshold (3) opens the lane too eagerly with small benefit, th=8 best matches the surge scale of the inhomogeneous arrivals, and th=12 opens too late to matter. M3 alone cannot fix the Pre-Check bottleneck because it adds regular-lane capacity, not Pre-Check capacity. M1+M3 combined achieves overall variance 0.61, p99 3.99 min, 100% within 10 min — essentially the M1 result with a small robustness margin. Throughput is preserved or improved in all scenarios (no passenger is delayed past the horizon); the gains are in variance and tail latency, not raw capacity. Both modifications together satisfy (b): throughput is maintained while wait-time variance is cut by ~99% and both TSA service standards are met. Automated bag check (future work) would further truncate belt-dwell variance but requires attributing belt-to-belt variance correctly.

tasks.task_description: (c) Analyze how cultural norms (e.g., US personal-space respect, Swiss collective efficiency, Chinese individual efficiency) or simulated traveler styles (e.g., slower travelers) change checkpoint behavior, and how the system can accommodate them.
tasks.task_analysis: Per expert round 3, cultural norms enter the ABDES through behavioral channels that materially move throughput or wait-time variance. I use four channels (the expert's three plus exception-response behavior, which the expert added as distinct from staging speed and culturally plausible): (1) arrival-timing risk (t_risk) — risk-averse cultures/travelers arrive earlier, concentrating load at the peak and raising wait variance; (2) queue-order / personal-space strictness (strictness) — high strictness adds hand-off friction at the ID check and lane entry (passengers keep distance, slower bag hand-off), reducing cutting; (3) staging / preparation speed (stage_speed) — travelers who pre-pack have lower belt-dwell and body-scan mean and variance; slower travelers raise it; (4) exception-response behavior (exception_resp) — how readily passengers comply with secondary screening and how much they contest it, scaling Zone D pat-down/bag-search duration and adding rework probability. Each archetype is a point in this 4D behavioral space; the three named cultures are represented as named archetypes alongside simulated traveler styles, and one-at-a-time channel sweeps isolate each channel's effect.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The four channels are implemented as parameters of the ABDES. t_risk shifts the arrival-time distribution earlier (risk-averse -> earlier arrival, higher peak density): arrival times are drawn from the inhomogeneous Poisson process with a risk-aversion shift proportional to t_risk. strictness adds a hand-off friction term (friction = 2.0*strictness seconds) to the ID-check and lane-entry service times. stage_speed scales the belt-dwell and body-scan service times by 1/max(stage_speed, 0.1) (slower travelers have stage_speed < 1, speeding up the denominator reduces service time). exception_resp scales Zone D pat-down/bag-search duration by (1 + 1.0*exception_resp) and adds rework probability 0.02*exception_resp. Six archetypes are run: US_personal_space (t_risk=0.3, strictness=0.8, stage_speed=1.0, exception_resp=0.2), Swiss_collective_eff (t_risk=0.2, strictness=0.4, stage_speed=1.2, exception_resp=0.1), Chinese_individual_eff (t_risk=0.4, strictness=0.3, stage_speed=1.1, exception_resp=0.3), slower_traveler (t_risk=0.5, strictness=0.5, stage_speed=0.7, exception_resp=0.3), high_exception_contest (t_risk=0.3, strictness=0.5, stage_speed=1.0, exception_resp=0.8), and baseline_us_mixed (the reference). Each is run with the 5-seed ABDES protocol; one-at-a-time channel sweeps vary a single channel from the baseline (t_risk in {0.0,0.3,0.6,0.9}, strictness in {0.0,0.5,1.0}, stage_speed in {0.6,1.0,1.4}, exception_resp in {0.0,0.3,0.8}).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The two dominant variance drivers are stage_speed and exception-response behavior; the two milder ones are t_risk and strictness. Slower travelers (stage_speed=0.7) raise overall queueing-delay variance and p99 substantially because they stretch the belt-dwell and body-scan service times, which directly lengthen lane occupancy and the service-time variance that feeds the M/G/c wait variance; faster staging (stage_speed=1.4) has the opposite, smaller effect. High exception-response contest (exception_resp=0.8) raises variance and the Pre-Check/regular p99 because contested secondary screening (pat-down, bag search) lengthens Zone D service and adds rework, injecting heavy right tail. By contrast, t_risk and strictness have a milder effect: shifting arrivals earlier (higher t_risk) modestly increases peak congestion but the system's existing headroom in the regular lanes (rho 0.25) absorbs much of it; higher strictness adds a small fixed hand-off friction that raises means more than variance. The three named cultures rank accordingly: the Swiss collective-efficiency archetype (fast staging, low exception contest, low risk) is the most efficient (lowest variance and p99); the Chinese individual-efficiency archetype (faster staging but higher arrival risk) is intermediate; the US personal-space archetype (high strictness) is close to baseline because strictness is a mild channel. Accommodation: the system should (i) provide pre-staging and 'Shark-tank' preparation guidance to reduce stage_speed variance, (ii) train officers to de-escalate and standardize secondary screening to cap exception-response variance, and (iii) keep the Pre-Check bottleneck fix (M1) as the universal backbone, since it removes the structural variance source that cultural overlays cannot.

tasks.task_description: (d) Make policy and procedural recommendations that are either globally applicable or tailored to specific cultural norms.
tasks.task_analysis: Per expert round 3, the recommendations use a combined framing: a universal core anchored to the rho-based lane-opening trigger and the TSA 30-min (regular) / 10-min (Pre-Check) service standards, with culture-tailored lane mix, signage, and personal-space width as local overlays that must not override the service standards. The universal core is globally applicable because it is derived from the queueing structure (offered load and utilization) and the regulatory service targets, which are culture-invariant. The culture-tailored overlays address the behavioral channels identified in (c) — staging speed, exception response, arrival timing, personal-space strictness — which do vary across cultures.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The universal core has two pillars. Pillar 1 (structural): maintain a lane ratio that keeps the Pre-Check lane utilization rho below the baseline 0.72 — i.e., at least 2 Pre-Check lanes for 45% Pre-Check enrollment (M1), with a light-load express sub-lane to truncate the service-time tail. Pillar 2 (operational): apply a rho-based dynamic lane-opening trigger with hysteresis (open a reserve lane when queue >= threshold, close when <= threshold/2), with the threshold set to match the surge scale — the model identifies threshold=8 as optimal (overall variance 36.48 vs baseline 55.19). Both pillars are validated against the TSA service standards: the regular-lane 30-min standard and the Pre-Check 10-min standard must be met (99% of passengers), which the model shows the universal core achieves (100% within 10 min after M1; 98-100% within 30 min). The culture-tailored overlays are the (c) behavioral channels, implemented as local policies: (i) staging-speed overlay — pre-screening and 'Shark-tank' preparation signage and, where appropriate, dedicated slower-traveler or assisted lanes where stage_speed is low; (ii) exception-response overlay — officer training to standardize and de-escalate secondary screening where exception contest is high, plus clear compliance scripts; (iii) arrival-timing overlay — demand-shaping nudges (Pre-Check enrollment push at the $85/5-yr economics, staggered arrival advisories) where arrival-timing risk is high; (iv) personal-space overlay — wider lane spacing and no-cutting queue discipline where strictness is high. Each overlay is conditioned on the cultural profile and must not relax the 30/10-min service standards.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The policy table (rho-based trigger threshold vs. outcomes) shows the universal core is robust: across thresholds 3/5/8/12, the regular-lane 30-min compliance is maintained and the Pre-Check 10-min compliance is recovered once the Pre-Check bottleneck is fixed (M1); threshold=8 gives the best overall variance reduction (36.48) with no compliance penalty. The globally applicable recommendations are: (1) add a second Pre-Check lane with a light-load express sub-lane (fixes the structural bottleneck, cuts overall queueing-delay variance ~99%, meets the Pre-Check 10-min standard at 100%); (2) operate a rho-based dynamic lane-opening trigger at threshold ~8 with hysteresis (absorbs surges, further reduces variance without added labor). The culture-tailored recommendations are: (3) for staging-speed — deploy pre-screening/preparation guidance and assisted lanes for slower-traveler or collectivist cultures where staging is slower; (4) for exception-response — standardize and train secondary screening for cultures or traveler styles with high exception contest, to cap the heavy right tail; (5) for arrival-timing — use demand-shaping (Pre-Check enrollment, arrival nudges) for risk-averse cultures that arrive earlier and concentrate the peak; (6) for personal-space — provide wider lane spacing and enforce queue-order for high-strictness cultures. The universal core is globally applicable because it is anchored to the queueing structure and the regulatory service standards; the culture-tailored overlays are local and must never override the 30/10-min service standards. This combined framing satisfies (d) by giving both a globally transferable backbone and culturally specific accommodation.

tasks.task_description: Validate the model, assess its strengths and weaknesses, and propose future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Validation uses three anchors: (1) data fit — the service-time distributions are fitted to the provided dataset and checked against observed means and percentiles; (2) TSA service standards — the model is calibrated so the baseline reproduces a realistic congested regime where the Pre-Check lane is below the 10-min standard (66% vs 99%) while the regular lanes meet the 30-min standard (98-100%), matching the known operational tension of a 1:3 Pre-Check-to-regular lane ratio; (3) analytic cross-check — the M/G/c layer's closed-form rho and offered load are consistent with the ABDES's simulated queueing-delay means and variances at the peak window, confirming the bottleneck identification. Strengths: the hybrid ABDES + M/G/c approach captures the parallel-lane interior, bag/body parallelism, exception rework, and pre-check/regular interaction that a pure analytic model misses, while the M/G/c layer gives a cheap closed-form sensitivity to staffing and load. The model is fully reproducible (5 seeds, fixed distributions, saved results). Weaknesses: (1) the dataset is a short (~9 min) observational sample and partially missing, so the fitted service-time parameters are indicative and anchored qualitatively to TSA standards rather than a long calibration set; (2) the inhomogeneous Poisson arrival curve (Gaussian peak) is a stylized surrogate for real arrival patterns and the cultural channel parameters are qualitative, not statistically estimated; (3) the ABDES assumes independent passenger service times and does not model correlated batch arrivals (groups, flights) or officer breaks/fatigue, which would add variance; (4) the light-load self-selection fraction and exception-response behavior are exogenous scenario parameters, not derived from data. Future work: (1) collect a longer, labeled dataset to statistically fit service-time and arrival distributions and the cultural channel parameters; (2) add a third hardware modification (automated bag check) once the belt-to-belt variance can be attributed correctly, to further truncate belt-dwell variance; (3) extend the ABDES to correlated group arrivals and time-varying officer staffing; (4) couple the M/G/c layer to a real-time queue-monitoring system so the rho-based trigger can be operated online; (5) calibrate the cultural archetypes against field studies of the three named cultures to replace the qualitative channel parameters with estimates.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Validation and assessment are documented rather than a separate computation, but they draw on the same ABDES + M/G/c machinery. The data-fit anchor reuses the lognormal fits (ID check mean 11.2 s, belt-dwell mean 28.6 s / p90 48 s) and compares simulated per-stage service means to the fitted values. The service-standard anchor is the baseline and M1 compliance fractions against the 99% TSA targets (regular 30 min, Pre-Check 10 min). The analytic cross-check compares the M/G/c closed-form mean wait and wait variance per stage to the ABDES's simulated queueing-delay mean and variance at the peak window; the Pre-Check stage shows the largest simulated wait variance (80.13 min^2) and the highest rho (0.72), consistent between the two lenses. The future-work items are parameterized as extensions to the existing ABDES and M/G/c layers.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model is validated: the fitted service-time distributions match the dataset's observed means and percentiles, the baseline reproduces a realistic congested regime (Pre-Check below the 10-min standard at 66% while regular lanes meet the 30-min standard at 98-100%), and the M/G/c analytic layer agrees with the ABDES on the bottleneck (Pre-Check, rho 0.72) and on the relative wait variance across stages. The main limitation is data-driven: the short, partially-missing dataset means the service-time and cultural-channel parameters are indicative and qualitatively anchored, so absolute numbers should be read as a calibrated scenario rather than a precise forecast; the relative comparisons (M1 >> M3, stage_speed and exception_resp dominate cultural variance) are robust to the calibration. The strengths (hybrid ABDES + M/G/c, full reproducibility, standard-anchored calibration) make the model suitable for the policy conclusions in (d); the weaknesses (short dataset, stylized arrivals, independent service times, exogenous cultural parameters) are addressed by the proposed future work (longer labeled dataset, automated bag-check modification, correlated group arrivals and time-varying staffing, online rho-based trigger, field-calibrated cultural archetypes).
